before: Once the recognition mechanism is clear, a candidate source list precedes HLA matching, target selection and product construction. Confirm alteration identity, tumour specificity and biological support first. DNA, RNA and protein answer different questions, and a longer list can add uncertain calls as well as genuine candidates. A DNA alteration can nominate a possible sequence without establishing the processed peptide that a conventional T cell will recognise.

For tumour DNA, retain local usable coverage, artefacts, tumour fraction and copy number with the call. For matched normal DNA, absence is conditional on suitable sampling, coverage and detection limits. Tumour RNA can support an altered transcript, but comes from a mixture of cells and depends on expression depth and processing. Protein or peptide detection is a further observation with its own method coverage, cell-of-origin question and detection limits; none of these measurements can simply stand in for the others.

A cancer-cell fraction estimate describes the sampled cancer cells, whereas truncal describes ancestry shared across sampled branches; a subclonal alteration belongs to a subset. One small biopsy need not establish the distribution across every site. Read fraction and ancestry do not show that a peptide is displayed, and an unobserved region or insufficiently sampled alteration remains a gap rather than a demonstrated negative.

In an invented comparison, candidate A has a supported tumour DNA alteration, no support in adequately assessed normal DNA and observed mutant RNA. It has progressed further as a source candidate, but processing, HLA display and T-cell recognition remain untested. Candidate B has tumour DNA support but inadequate normal coverage, so tumour specificity is still unresolved. These are evidence questions, not a numerical ranking algorithm.

Two more fictional candidates illustrate bounded negatives. Candidate C has only a weakly supported RNA junction and needs reproducibility and artefact checks. Candidate D has strong DNA support but no RNA detection in a shallow assay, which cannot establish that the transcript is absent. None of A to D has demonstrated HLA presentation or T-cell recognition merely from these starting observations.

Prepared specimens and analysis can introduce misleading candidates through fixation damage, contamination, misalignment or uncertain junctions. The chosen reference transcript also matters when translating an altered sequence. Preserve specimen identity, coordinates and alleles, transcript/reference, method and software versions, usable coverage, thresholds and manual decisions so the result can be traced to its source. A filter or annotation is not independent proof of function.

Parkhurst and colleagues found neoantigen-reactive cultured lymphocyte populations in 62 of 75 people with gastrointestinal cancers. About 1.6% of the tested protein-changing mutant gene products were recognised, and 99% of the recognised determinants were unique to one person. This is a selected study and assay result, not the probability that any mutation is processed, displayed or useful in breast cancer. Applying 0.016 to 60 fictional candidate mutations gives 0.96, about one, as an arithmetic illustration only.

In a fictional comparison, the same expressed mutation produces a nine-amino-acid peptide that is displayed by person A's HLA-A*02:01 and meets a matching receptor. Person B's tested classical class-I variants bind no mutation-spanning peptide adequately; a possible class-II response is a different question. If A's tumour later loses the required HLA allele, the mutation can remain while that recognition route fails. Several candidates sharing that allele do not provide independent protection. Tumour-specific sequence also does not guarantee that its receptor avoids unrelated healthy-tissue targets.

Compare a fictional normal protein with an altered version that differs at one marked position. A fragment spanning that position is an altered sequence candidate; the mutation label alone does not specify its boundaries or show that it reaches HLA. Several overlapping fragments can contain the change, while none may turn out to be naturally displayed and recognised. Ask separately whether the source is expressed and processed, whether the relevant HLA displays it, and whether a compatible receptor responds. If fictional candidate A has a favourable prediction and B is recognised on naturally presenting tumour cells with suitable controls, B has more direct recognition evidence for those cells and conditions. changes.purpose: Self-contained matched normal/altered candidate and evidence-gate exercise; fictional premises, no real sequence or clinical performance number.

before: Central and peripheral tolerance include distinct mechanisms. Kisielow and colleagues demonstrated deletion of self-reactive developing cells in an H-Y-receptor transgenic mouse model. Jenkins and Schwartz demonstrated antigen-related unresponsiveness after altered antigen presentation in mouse experiments, and Sakaguchi and colleagues linked a CD4/CD25 regulatory population to prevention of autoimmunity in mice. These are mechanistic examples, rather than universal human response or safety thresholds. A tumour-specific mutation can make a peptide distinguishable from its normal counterpart, but display and a responsive receptor are still needed, and there is no universal percentage of identity that makes a target safe. Higher receptor affinity is not automatically more selective. Receptors can cross-react with peptides from unrelated proteins, as in the titin peptide recognised by the MAGE-A3-directed receptor (Cameron et al., 2013, PMID 23926201; Linette et al., 2013, PMID 23770775). Luksza et al. (Nature 2022, PMID 35589842) modelled neoantigen quality, using non-selfness and selfness, in pancreatic cancer survivors; the model is not a clinical safety rule. In a loaded-peptide concentration series, compare mutant and normal peptides at the same concentration with the same HLA and responder; artificial loading leaves natural processing open and a response threshold is not a patient safety threshold.

In a fictional loaded peptide assay, the same receptor and matching HLA are tested at 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 nanomolar with a 24 hour activation endpoint. Mutant peptide M gives 5%, 28%, 70% and 90% activated responder cells; normal peptide N gives 3%, 18%, 61% and 86%. Each percentage divides activated cells by viable responder cells in that condition, and the invented no peptide background is 2%. Equal horizontal spacing represents tenfold concentration steps on a logarithmic axis; straight lines only connect the four stated points. These are invented teaching values, with no supplied replicates or uncertainty estimates, and are not data from Cameron or another study.

Under those fictional premises, the receptor responds to both M and N, so the sequence distinction has not produced exclusive receptor recognition in this assay. Artificial loading leaves natural processing and display open. A second receptor responding to M but not N would be more discriminating under the tested conditions; one negative response would not establish absence of recognition at another concentration, with another preparation or in every healthy tissue. Keep the normal counterpart, plausible cross reactive targets, relevant healthy cell systems and assay controls in view. Neither a response concentration nor a sequence similarity score is a patient safety threshold.
